ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The circuit has three main nodes: upper, middle, and lower. On the left is a 1 mA DC current source, with the arrow upward, connected between the lower node and the upper node. On the right there are two series-connected 2 kΩ resistors; the upper 2 kΩ is connected between the upper node and the middle node, and the lower 2 kΩ is connected between the middle node and the lower node. The middle vertical branch has two ideal diodes: D1 is between the upper node and the middle node, and D2 is between the middle node and the lower node; in the figure, D1 and D2 are oriented oppositely, and the marked current I is the downward current through the D2 branch. Reasoning: First temporarily ignore the diode conduction states and look only at the two 2 kΩ series resistors on the right, whose equivalent is 4 kΩ. The 1 mA current source sends current into the upper node, so the current flows through the resistor string from top to bottom, giving the upper node potential higher than the middle node, and the middle node potential higher than the lower node. According to the diode orientations in the figure, the forward direction of D1 is from the upper node to the middle node, so D1 is forward biased; the forward direction of D2 is from the lower node to the middle node, so when the middle node is higher than the lower node, D2 is reverse biased. Under ideal diodes, D1 is equivalent to a short circuit, and D2 is equivalent to an open circuit. Therefore the D2 branch has no current, and the marked downward current I = 0 mA.
